You want to know about the history project, Uday? Fine. It's not a proud story.

I'm Ritu, and I was made group leader for a model of the Harappan city. Four of us. On day one I looked at everyone's rough sketches and thought, these are messy, I'll just do it myself.

So I did. Every night for two weeks I was up till one, cutting cardboard, painting drains, writing the chart. In class I told the others, "It's handled, relax."

By the last week I was falling asleep in maths. My hands shook when I glued the roofs. The drains I painted at 2 am were crooked.

We got a C. And the worst part was at the viva: the teacher asked the others how the drainage worked, and they couldn't answer. They'd never touched it. One of them said, "Ritu didn't let us."

qa.a: The model got a C.

qa.a: Ritu felt ashamed and stung, realising the others had been shut out rather than lazy.

qa.q: What approach could Ritu have used instead of doing it all alone?
qa.a: Ritu could have given each person one part with a check-in to review quality, so work was shared and everyone learned the drainage system.

qa.a: They likely felt sidelined and a little resentful, unable to answer at the viva because they were never allowed to touch the work.

I'm Tanvir, Simran's neighbour in the hostel. For three weeks before our Class 11 geography project was due, her light was on past midnight almost every night. I could see it under the door.

Once I knocked to borrow a charger. Her desk was covered in maps, glue and three laptops' worth of printouts. "Where's your group?" I asked. "Sleeping. It's faster if I do it," she said, not looking up.

In the mess, her group members sat together laughing. When a teacher asked one of them about the rainfall chart, the girl shrugged and said, "Simran's doing that."

The day before submission, Simran came to breakfast with red eyes and dropped her plate. The model looked fine from far away, but the labels were misspelt.

I don't know how she felt. She didn't talk much that week.

Nobody met again. There was always another test.

In the final week, Dolma called everyone to her flat. Farida came. Two others didn't: one had a fever, and one was at a family wedding in Nashik.

Dolma and Farida worked late on two evenings with cardboard and foil. The reflector kept slipping. They taped it at a strange angle. On the day, the teacher tested it in the sun and it barely warmed the water.

Farida said quietly on the way out, "We had six weeks, Dolma."

Our Class 10 team project last year was a model of a smart streetlight, and honestly, the thing that saved it wasn't the circuit. It was a rule.

In the first meeting, Salma, who led the group, tapped her pen and said, "Two check-ins a week, Tuesday and Friday, ten minutes in the library corner. And one rule: if you're stuck, you say it the same day in the group chat. No hiding."

I'm Kiran, and I was the one who got stuck first. The light sensor wouldn't respond, and I was embarrassed to admit it. But the rule was the rule, so I posted, "Sensor dead, don't know why." Salma replied in five minutes, and Tuesday we found the wire in the wrong pin.

Without that rule I'd have fiddled alone till the last week. Instead, we submitted four days early, and I actually slept the night before.

qa.a: The check-ins were on Tuesday and Friday, ten minutes in the library corner.

Naveen and Jaya's group of five began badly: in week one, two members did not know what the others were building. I suggested they agree on a routine before touching any wires.

They wrote their own rules on a chart paper and stuck it in the lab: a ten-minute check-in every Monday and Thursday at lunch; one chat group for all updates; and "if stuck, say so within a day".

In week three, Jaya posted that the motor they ordered would arrive late. Because it came out on Thursday and not the night before submission, Naveen found a spare in the junior lab.

I sat in on two check-ins. They were short, sometimes silly, but everyone spoke. I have asked the group to share their chart with the other project teams next week.

In the robotics club room, Francis tapped the whiteboard with his marker. "Four legs, not wheels. It'll climb the ramp easily. Trust me."

Alka had doubts. Legs were hard to balance. She glanced at Jomon, who looked unsure too. But Francis sounded so certain, and everyone else was already nodding.

"Sounds great," Alka said.

For three weeks they built legs. Nobody raised the balance problem again.

On test day, the robot took two steps up the ramp, tipped sideways and fell off the table. One leg snapped.

Later, eating biscuits in silence, Jomon finally said, "I thought legs were a bad idea from the start."

"Me too," Alka admitted.

Francis stared. "Why didn't you say anything?"

"You seemed so sure," Alka said. "Nobody wanted to go first."

The coach, packing up, said only, "Next time, someone has to be."

Dear Joseph,

You asked how the bridge competition went. Badly. And I want to tell you why, because I think it was partly my fault.

Rohit was so confident. He said a single arch of ice-cream sticks would hold five kilos, no need for side trusses. I thought the arch alone looked weak. So did Nilesh, I found out later. But Rohit had won last year, and when he asked, "Everyone okay?", we all said yes.

At testing, the bridge cracked at two kilos. The judges were kind about it, which was worse.

On the bus back, Nilesh said, "I knew it would bend." I said, "Me too." Rohit went very quiet.

We agreed with him because arguing felt awkward. That awkwardness cost us the whole competition. Next time I'll say it, even if my voice shakes.

Imran

After their water filter failed at the first trial, I expected the team to argue about blame. Instead, their captain, Amandeep, asked each of the five to name one concern about the next design, going round the circle. Nobody was allowed to pass.

Pooja, who had stayed silent in the first round, cleared her throat and said the charcoal layer was too thin. Another said the budget was nearly gone.

Amandeep then drew a table on the board with three columns: cost, time and how likely it was to work. The team scored three ideas out of five on each. The clay-pot filter scored lowest on cost and highest overall, though it was nobody's favourite at the start.

I watched them build it in eight days. It passed the second trial. I have asked Amandeep to explain the scoring table at our next club meeting.

Our first bird feeder design failed on Tuesday. Squirrels ate everything in an hour. Everyone had agreed with Vandana's idea because she spoke first and loudest. I did too.

So today, as leader, I tried something different. I asked everyone to say one worry about any design before we chose. Out loud, one by one.

Vandana went first and said her own design was too open. Then Rishi said the second idea needed wood we couldn't afford. Kavita worried about time because of exams.

Then I made a quick table in my notebook: cost, time, will it work. Scores from one to five. The hanging bottle feeder won, and it was Kavita's quiet idea from Tuesday that nobody had listened to.

I'm Minakshi, and I felt nervous running it that way. But it felt fairer, and less like a popularity vote.

Mehek's group made another page about me. Third one this month. They wrote under my class photo that I smell and nobody should sit next to me.

For weeks I just felt sick and couldn't explain it to anyone. It felt like fog. Alka, my cousin, said, "Dilnaz, write it down. Dates, what they wrote, screenshots. Then it's not a feeling, it's a list."

So tonight I did. 3 Sept: comment on my photo. 11 Sept: fake page. 19 Sept: voice note mocking my accent. Today: new page. Twelve screenshots in a folder.

Seeing it on paper, I finally understood it wasn't me being sensitive. It was a pattern.

After dinner I showed Ammi the list. She read every line, held my hand, and said, "None of this is your fault." Then she emailed my class teacher and the counsellor with the screenshots before we slept.

qa.a: Twelve screenshots in a folder.

qa.a: Dilnaz felt clearer and less alone, relieved to see it as a real pattern rather than being too sensitive.

qa.a: The school counsellor and class teacher should follow up with Dilnaz and Ammi and act under the school's anti-bullying rules, while Dilnaz keeps adding any new incidents to the list.

qa.a: Ammi was probably hurt and protective, which shows in holding Dilnaz's hand, saying it was not Dilnaz's fault and emailing the school that night.

The next morning she went with him to see his class teacher, Mr. Lindqvist, before first lesson. He read the list too, then asked Emil a few quiet questions. "I'm bringing in the school counsellor today," he said. "We have a plan for exactly this."

By Friday afternoon, the counsellor had met Emil, the boys' parents had been called, and the teacher had moved Emil's locker.

Emil slept better that night than he had in weeks.
